vignette:
Omar presents as a man hollowed out by exhaustion. At 54, his work as a community organizer has been his life's purpose, but for the last eighteen months, he has felt himself receding from it, becoming a ghost in his own life. The change began the night his then-partner of two years attacked him in their shared apartment. The assault was a blur of confusion and pain, happening late at night in the near-total darkness of their bedroom. He remembers very little in a coherent sequence, only disconnected pieces: the sudden shift in his partner's tone, the sound of a lamp shattering, and the persistent, rhythmic thump-thump-thump of a news helicopter that had been circling a nearby traffic accident, a sound that seemed to drill directly into his skull.

This fragmented memory is now the central organizing principle of his life. The belief that he was profoundly betrayed by someone he trusted has become a constant internal monologue, a question he tortures himself with: how could he not have seen it coming? This sense of personal failure fuels his rumination, forcing him to sift through the broken shards of memory for an explanation, which only serves to keep the trauma fresh and immediate. He has come to believe the event happened because of an essential weakness in his character, a flaw that makes him a target. This conviction has poisoned his perception of the world, shattering his long-held belief in community and mutual trust. Now, he sees potential threats everywhere, making him exquisitely sensitive to reminders of the trauma.

The city itself has become a minefield. The percussive sound of any helicopter passing over his office is enough to trigger a flashback, yanking him from a meeting and back into that dark room. When this happens, the memory arrives without warning, a full-sensory replay of auditory fragments-the sound of his own ragged breathing, the phantom thumping of the blades in his ears. Each time these sounds break through, it feels like irrefutable proof of his own powerlessness, reinforcing his conviction that he is fundamentally weak and an easy target. Because the memory exists not as a coherent story but as these raw, decontextualized sounds, his mind is constantly on alert for anything that might herald its return, making him acutely sensitive to the ambient noise of the city. These intrusive experiences have conditioned a powerful fear response. Because the memories feel so real and present, he has developed strategies to keep them at bay. He began avoiding the entire neighborhood where the assault took place, a significant challenge given his work often requires him to be in that part of the city. This avoidance, while providing momentary relief, only reinforces his belief that he is broken and incapable, strengthening the very self-blame that keeps the cycle going.

The constant threat of re-experiencing the trauma has also led him to change how he carries himself in the world. He finds himself constantly scanning faces in the subway, on the street, assessing everyone for signs of danger. This hypervigilance makes him more likely to notice things that might act as a trigger, like a dark alleyway he must pass on his way to a community center, which now feels charged with menace. He has started wearing deep-hooded sweatshirts and a baseball cap, even indoors, in an effort to feel invisible. He believes that by concealing himself, he can avoid being noticed and therefore avoid danger. Yet, this strategy of hiding only deepens his appraisal of himself as a damaged person who must be kept out of sight, further cementing his sense of shame and isolation.

The feedback loop is now all-consuming. The intrusive memories dictate his behaviors, and the behaviors confirm his darkest beliefs about himself and the world. His work, which relies on his ability to connect with people and move freely through the city, has suffered immensely. He has missed important meetings because they were held in buildings near the avoided neighborhood. His constant state of high alert leaves him drained and unable to be present with his community members, or even with his husband at home. He finally sought therapy after his husband found him frozen in their apartment's dark hallway, paralyzed with fear after a helicopter passed overhead. Omar's hope is faint, but it is there: he wants to be able to walk through his own city without fear and, more than anything, to silence the internal voice that tells him he is to blame.
